AKM Nazrul Islam with Jeban Naher Ayesha, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner 
MA Tariq with A H Khondaker, Advocates ----- For Respondent No.2.

Mostafa Miah ----- Petitioner
Vs.

full_judgment:
Habibur Rahman Khan,J.: On an application filed by Md. Mostafa Miah a Rule Nisi was issued calling upon the respondents to show cause as to why the decision and order dated 11.11.91 passed by the First Labour Court, Dhaka in complaint case No. 37 of 1990 as evidenced by Annexure-L to the petition moved in Court today, should not be declared to have been made without any lawful authority and to be of no legal effect or such other or further order or orders passed as to this Court may seem fit and proper. 

 3. Thereafter one Md. Jahangir Alam, was appointed as Administrative Officer (Investigation) for holding enquiry and the petitioner was found guilty of the charges brought against him. Consequently by the report of the enquiry officer, Bangladesh Biman issued a second show cause notice on 28.1.90 to the petitioner and the petitioner gave a reply to the said show cause notice denying the charges. Bangladesh Biman Authority by its order dated 19.2.90 dismissed the petitioner from his service. Being aggrieved by the order of dismissal the petitioner filed a grievance petition on 4.3.90 but did not receive any reply to his grievance petition from Bangladesh Biman Authority. The petitioner thereafter filed the Complaint Case No. 37 of 1990 before the 1st Labour Court, Dhaka under section 25(1)(b) of the Standing Orders Act, 1965 against the order of dismissal of the petitioner from his service on 19.2.90 with a prayer for reinstating him in his service with all back wages. In the complaint case the petitioner as 1st party stated that the dismissal order having been passed on 19.2.90 was received by him on the same day and the petitioner served the grievance petition on 4.3.90 but he did not receive any reply. It was alleged that the dismissal order was mala fide and arbitrary and violative of Biman Service Regulations and General Law of the country and also is a colorable exercise of power and has been made with malafide motive. In the petition of complaint it was also stated that Bangladesh Biman having published advertisement in the Bangladesh Times on 18.5.89 inviting tender for selling two of used/old cars numbering Dhaka Cha-4095 and Chittagong Kha-3130 by auction, the owner of the Kazi and Kazi Motors, 77, Bijoynagar, Dhaka offered a tender for buying the two cars and the last day of offering the tender was on 11.6.89 on which day Mr. Kazi Md. Jasimuddin was very busy. Being morally pressed the petitioner offered tender on 11.6.89 on behalf of his friend the proprietor of M/s. Kazi and Kazi Motors during his off duty. The petitioner neither had the means to buy an old/used car, nor did he make a financial gain out of the transaction and M/s. Kazi and Kazi Motors took delivery of the used car No. Chittagong Kha-3130 and did not take delivery of the other car. 

 4. The respondents filed written statement before the Labour Court challenging the maintainability of the complaint case stating that the petition of the 1st party petitioner was misconceived and he has got no cause of action as he was lawfully dismissed from his service and as such he is not entitled to get any relief as prayed for. It was further stated that notice to show cause was issued to the 1st party but he did not reply to the show cause notice acceptable by the second party. The learned Labour Court by his order dated 11.11.91 dismissed the case on contest. Being aggrieved the 1st party as petitioner has filed this application under Article 102 of the Constitution and has obtained the instant Rule. 

 5. Mr. AKM Nazrul Islam, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, after taking us through the judgment of the Labour Court, submits that the petitioner had not committed any misconduct as per Biman Service Regulations and the allegations made in the charge sheet on the very face of it do not constitute any misconduct so as to bring the same within the mischief of section 55(2) of the Biman Service Regulations. The learned Advocate submits that the petitioner only assisted his friend, the proprietor of M/s, Kazi and Kazi Motors, with regard to his offering tender in his absence being pressed by moral duty and he neither obtained the car for himself nor made any financial gain out of the transaction and M/s. Kazi and Kazi Motors took delivery of one used car and did not take delivery of the other car. The learned Advocate submits that purchase of the car in the name of another, even if it is proved, cannot be treated as an offence of misconduct or corrupt practice as defined under Regulation 55, as the petitioner being the citizen of the country has the constitutional rights to acquire, hold, transfer or otherwise dispose of the property as defined under Article 42 of the Constitution and, as such, this cannot be a ground for awarding punishment dismissing the petitioner from service. The next point urged by the learned Advocate is, that the enquiry was not held legally and properly and the petitioner was not furnished with the copy of the enquiry report along with the second show cause notice so as to enable him to answer the charges properly and in that view of the mauer the impugned order of dismissal is without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. 

 6. Mr. Amir Hossain Khandker, the learned Advocate with Mr. MA Tariq, appearing for the respondents, submits that the petitioner being the employee of Bangladesh Biman is to be guided by the Employees Service Regulations, 1979 and he having dealt with the disposal of the car of Biman by way of holding auction and the same being related to financial deal comes within the mischief of. Regulation 55 and hence the authority after holding enquiry-observing all formalities having found him guilty-awarded the punishment which he deserved. With regard to the service of the copy of enquiry committee's report the learned Advocate for the respondent submits that non-service of Enquiry Committee's report has not in any way caused prejudice to the petitioner and affected the enquiry which was held duly and properly and in that view of the matter the petitioner is not entitled to get any relief in the writ application. With regard to the next point, urged that the past service record of the petitioner has not been taken into consideration by the authority before the major penalty was awarded by the authority. The learned Advocate for the respondent submits that it is not a legal requirement and hence non-compliance of the same has not in any way vitiated the enquiry and the order of dismissal from service was passed by the authority after consideration of the enquiry report. The last point submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner to the effect that the facts and circumstances of another case being Complaint Case No. 36 of 1990 has been mixed up together and this shows the non-application of judicial mind of the learned Court. The learned Advocate for the respondent having pointed out the judgment and order of the learned Labour Court submits that though reference has been made in respect of another case but that has not weighed the mind of the learned Labour Court in arriving at the decision with regard to the present case of the petitioner. On perusal of the judgment we find no substance in the point submitted by the learned Advocate for the petitioner. Now let us come to the point of not furnishing the enquiry report along with the second show cause notice issued by the respondents to the petitioner. Though there is no provision in the Bangladesh Biman Corporation Employees (Service) Regulations, 1979 for service of any show cause notice but in the instant case second show cause notice is admittedly served and issued on the petitioner. Second show cause notice is, in fact, the accused employee's last opportunity to place his side of the case before the appointing authority who is about to take the last decision with regard to the punishment to be awarded against the employee and accordingly, it has been held in the case of Md. Torab Ali Vs. Bangladesh Textile Mills Corporation and another reported in 1989 BLD 383 (relevant page 386) that the accused employee has the burden of disabusing the mind of the appointing authority from the impression created by the report of the enquiry officer. In the instant case we have already seen that the second show cause notice was served by the authority to the petitioner but the question is whether non-receipt of the report by the petitioner has caused any prejudice to him in making proper representation to the authority so far the punishment sought to be inflicted on him. In the present case as the petitioner did not get the copy of the report he had not the means of knowing what finding or findings of the enquiry officer have gone against him and what have weighed the mind of the appointing authority in coming to a decision as to the punishment proposed to be inflicted upon him. Therefore, it has been held in the above referred to case that the second show cause notice no doubt requires the delinquent to show cause why the proposed punishment shall not be inflicted upon him but upon perusal of his reply the appointing authority may still take any view with regard to the proposed punishment to be awarded. In order to be meaningful it has to be furnished along with the report of the Enquiry Officer. 

 7. Relying on the decision cited above we also hold that, whether or not rules or regulations provide for a copy of the report to be given to the employee, the rules of natural justice requires that along with the second show cause notice the petitioner should have been furnished with the report. In the present case the report having not been furnished to the petitioner along with the report affording him the opportunity to show cause against the proposed punishment, which was admittedly a major penalty like dismissal from service, the order passed by the respondent dismissing the petitioner from service cannot be sustained. 

 "In awarding punishment under this Act the employer shall take into account the gravity of the misconduct, the previous record, if any, of the worker and any other extenuating or aggravating circumstances that may exist." 

 9. On perusal of the records it is apparently found that the requirement of sub-section 6 of section 18 of the Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act has not been complied with, though it is obligatory on the part of the employer to take into consideration the gravity of misconduct and the previous record of the worker, if there be any. Though the compliance of provisions of sub-section 6 of section 18 of Employment of Labour (Standing Orders) Act is obligatory, in the case of Adamjee Jute Mills Ltd. Vs. Chairman 3rd Labour Court and another reported in 12 DLR 371, it was held: 

 In the present case the other papers do not show that the previous record has been considered for the purpose of awarding punishment; from the impugned order Annexure-H it has also been found that the learned Labour Court has observed that in case of awarding the major punishment such as dismissal from service upon a worker, the employer has an obligation to consider extenuating circumstances such as period of service, and previous service record, etc. of the delinquent worker under section 18(6) of the (Standing Orders) Act 1965. In spite of such observation made by the learned Labour Court the order of dismissal which is a major punishment has been upheld on dismissal of the complaint case filed by the petitioner. As the order of dismissal has been upheld the opinion expressed by the learned Labour Court that the authority instead of dismissing the 1st party from service could impose lesser punishment as provided under section 56(b)(c) & (d) of the Bangladesh Biman Corporation Employees (Service) Regulations, 1979 has remained a pious wish only.
